tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: NATIVE TARGET ZONE: gallery photo 1 Cleveland Powell's green source-identified attached flowering head from Comfort, Kendall County, photo 2 Eric Knight's ripe rust-tan tight heads from Brady, McCulloch County. Both are exact-source and individually CC BY. Gallery photo 3 has the original California tiny live aboveground tuft; photo 7 Matt Lavin's Utah standing plant; photo 11 is Bob Harms' credited external Central Texas collected dried annual with visible roots. Neither new Texas photo exposes roots or proves perennial-vs-annual anatomy.
tiles.status: TEXAS FLOWERING STAGES PHOTOGRAPHED; CONNECTED TRUE ROOT BASE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · COUNT ONE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Local Texas-source fresh and ripe sixweeks awned heads are now in panels 1–2, others in panels 4–5 and 8; compare with entirely DIFFERENT species Texas fescue (gallery 14) before counting and dissecting a mature 5–17-flowered sixweeks spikelet. Finger photos are NOT mm-calibrated floret measurements.

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO UNEQUAL GLUMES
tiles.details: The isolated tiny fragment in gallery panel 4 is NOT a confirmed glume! Still need intact mature spikelet and controlled dissection separating first 1-veined lower and 3-veined upper glumes; calibrated macro mandatory.

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA & REAL AWN
tiles.details: Fertile lemma body 2.7–6.5 mm, five-veined, ending in one actual awn about 0.3–6 mm in Kew GrassBase. Do not include the awn when measuring lemma body or mistake the pointed upper glume for the lemma awn. Awned units are visible, but insertion/veins remain unverified.

tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE COLLAR
tiles.details: Peel blade from sheath and photograph the inner blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm scale. The short hairless-edged membranous ligule is not the blade tip, sheath edge or a loose hair. No current panel proves its length.
tiles.status: TRUE LIGULE STILL MISSING — no aboveground head, open shoot or comparable fescue photograph proves the free 0.5–1 mm membrane

tiles.heading: 06 · SPLIT THE FESCUES
tiles.details: GALLERY 1–2 show actual attached green and ripe sixweeks heads from Comfort and Brady (Texas). GALLERY 13–14 show DIFFERENT SPECIES perennial Texas fescue's living leafy tuft and single mature whole spikelet from existing canonical sources, not sixweeks fescue. Contrast sixweeks annual narrow many-flowered awned heads with Texas fescue open drooping panicle and few-flowered shorter-awns/awnless spikelet. Same-root annual-vs-perennial growth proof and measured dissection remain absent; NEVER count Texas fescue panels as sixweeks source anatomy.
tiles.status: REAL SIDE-BY-SIDE DIFFERENT-SPECIES CC BY PHOTO COMPARISON; ROOT AND LIGULE GAPS HELD

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: SIXWEEKS FESCUE — FIRST find a short-lived cool-season ANNUAL with shallow fibrous roots, threadlike rolled/folded blades about 0.5–1 mm wide, and a narrow usually contracted 1–20 cm panicle. Under a lens count 5–17 florets in one 4–10 mm spikelet, not spikelets in the panicle. Lower glume 1.7–4.5 mm/1 vein; upper glume 2.7–6.7 mm/3 veins; fertile lemma 2.7–6.5 mm/5 veins, ending in a real 0.3–6 mm awn. True ligule a very short 0.5–1 mm hairless-edged membrane. Compare the larger, persistent PERENNIAL Texas fescue with 2–4-flowered, awnless/mucronate spikelets; source photographs do not prove the hidden root or ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FROM A FEW FEET AWAY look for a very small, short-lived cool-season grass with fine rolled or folded blades and a narrow, crowded awned panicle. Start with REAL Texas source photos in panels 1–2 (indices 0–1), then in-situ Utah plant in panel 7 (index 6). A photographed dry clump alone does not prove lifespan.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Peel blade from sheath and photograph the inner blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm scale. The short hairless-edged membranous ligule is not the blade tip, sheath edge or a loose hair. No current panel proves its length.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Local Texas-source fresh and ripe sixweeks awned heads are now in panels 1–2, others in panels 4–5 and 8; compare with entirely DIFFERENT species Texas fescue (gallery 14) before counting and dissecting a mature 5–17-flowered sixweeks spikelet. Finger photos are NOT mm-calibrated floret measurements.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Festuca versuta (Texas fescue) is a perennial rather than a 6-weeks spring annual, with a more open branching flowering panicle in mature plants and a persistent base. The existing F. versuta image is loose seed/lemma material, so it does not prove panicle or perennial habit. For other Vulpia spp., dissect unequal glumes and measure lemma and awn instead of using dried color.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: The small upright grass grows from one low base on dry rock/sand. Slender leaves and a number of narrow, mostly erect flowering branches rise above the base. It shows a single-season SIZE AND HABIT candidate; this photo alone cannot prove lifespan or ligule size.

panels.label: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Texas fescue multi-flowered spikelet
panels.caption: Texas fescue has shorter usually few-flowered spikelets in its published treatment, often without a long projecting awn, unlike sixweeks fescue's crowded often 5–17-flowered awned units. This source photograph is a whole spikelet, not a calibrated dissection or independently counted florets.

intro: SIXWEEKS FESCUE — FIRST find a short-lived cool-season ANNUAL with shallow fibrous roots, threadlike rolled/folded blades about 0.5–1 mm wide, and a narrow usually contracted 1–20 cm panicle. Under a lens count 5–17 florets in one 4–10 mm spikelet, not spikelets in the panicle. Lower glume 1.7–4.5 mm/1 vein; upper glume 2.7–6.7 mm/3 veins; fertile lemma 2.7–6.5 mm/5 veins, ending in a real 0.3–6 mm awn. True ligule a very short 0.5–1 mm hairless-edged membrane. Compare the larger, persistent PERENNIAL Texas fescue with 2–4-flowered, awnless/mucronate spikelets; source photographs do not prove the hidden root or ligule.
memory_rule: Annual sixweeks: small one-season plant, narrowly crowded AWNED spikelets usually with multiple florets. Texas fescue: a perennial with a looser flowering panicle and relatively few florets, often lacking extended awns. A single dead tuft is not sufficient proof of life cycle.
safety_note: Ten local exact-species files; two additional Harms exact-species images are external credited educational-use only, NOT CC; two gallery panels depict different F. versuta. California/Utah source localities do not verify Hays County occurrence. Do not claim true ligule or glume veins are visible.
field_rule: Small short-lived annual + narrow crowded many-flowered awned panicle suggests F. octoflora; verify unequal glumes, five-veined fertile lemma, true ligule and rooted growth form on the same specimen to distinguish similar fescues.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Festuca versuta (Texas fescue) is a perennial rather than a 6-weeks spring annual, with a more open branching flowering panicle in mature plants and a persistent base. The existing F. versuta image is loose seed/lemma material, so it does not prove panicle or perennial habit. For other Vulpia spp., dissect unequal glumes and measure lemma and awn instead of using dried color.
